title: The days of distress (Mark 13:14–27)
hook: strange apocalyptic images; Christians read them in several ways

segments.voice: Yesterday, not one stone left on another, and your line was don't worry beforehand. Did you catch yourself rehearsing tomorrow? Day two hundred sixteen.

Some parts of the Bible read like a letter from a friend. This part reads like a dream you can't quite explain the next morning. Still on the Mount of Olives, Jesus goes on. When you see a terrible thing standing where it shouldn't, run. Whoever is on the roof, don't go down to fetch anything. Whoever is in the field, don't go back for your coat. Pray it doesn't happen in winter. Then the sky itself seems to come apart: sun darkened, moon gone dim, stars falling. And in the middle of all this, Mark does something he never does anywhere else. He turns to you, the reader, directly, with a little aside in brackets. In the King James Bible: "let him that readeth understand." In other words: pay attention. This is for you.
screen: `LIKE A DREAM YOU CAN'T EXPLAIN.` → `RUN. DON'T GO BACK.` → `LET HIM THAT READETH UNDERSTAND.`

segments.voice: The terrible thing is called the abomination of desolation, a phrase from the book of Daniel. When Daniel was written, it pointed to a real event: a foreign king, Antiochus, set up a pagan altar in the temple, about two centuries before Jesus. Jews remember the temple's rededication after that at Hanukkah. Jesus borrows the old phrase for a new disaster. Then the cosmic images: the sun darkened, the moon not giving her light, stars falling. Israel's prophets used pictures like these for the fall of empires. And then: they'll see the Son of man coming in the clouds with great power and glory, another picture from Daniel, and he'll gather his chosen from the four winds, from one end of the earth to the other. So what does it mean? Christians read it in several ways, and sincere believers land in different places. Many scholars and churches read the first part as about the Roman war and the temple's fall in the year 70. Most Christians read the coming in the clouds as about Christ's return at the end of time, which the old creeds confess: he will come again. Some read nearly all of it as already fulfilled in 70. Others read it as still ahead, a future time of trouble. Mark doesn't settle it, but he keeps coming back to two things. Don't be deceived by people with confident timelines. And later in this same speech, a promise: "Heaven and earth shall pass away: but my words shall not pass away." Whatever the images mean, the speaker's words are meant to be the one steady thing when everything else shakes.
screen: `DANIEL'S ABOMINATION OF DESOLATION.` · `A SKY COMING APART.` · `THE SON OF MAN IN THE CLOUDS.` · `SEVERAL READINGS, ONE PROMISE.` · then, large: `MY WORDS SHALL NOT PASS AWAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read slowly, without fear. Settle, and breathe. Take one line and let it be the steady thing: heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away. Breathe in on the first half. Out on the second. If frightening pictures come, from this chapter, or the news, or your own worries, notice them, and come back to the line. You don't have to decode anything today. If you pray, you can rest your fear in that promise. The bell holds the time.
The days of distress. Strange images of flight and falling stars, which Christians read in several ways, around one steady promise.
Your line: my words won't pass away. Today, when a scary headline grabs you, read it slowly, breathe, and hold on to something that lasts. Day two hundred sixteen.

howItsDone: Christians confess in the Nicene Creed that Christ "will come again"; churches read this chapter especially in Advent, and interpret its images in several ways, from the fall of the temple in 70 to Christ's return at the end of time.

fork.setup: you're a first reader of Mark. you hear of the abomination of desolation standing where it ought not. what does the text tell you to do?
options: flee to the mountains and don't go back.
fork.reveal: flee: from the roof, from the field, don't go back even for a coat. and don't trust anyone with a confident timeline.

original.note: Greek: an abomination, something detestable. from Daniel's phrase, the abomination of desolation.

trapdoor: what you thought: a map of the end of the world.
what it means: dream-like pictures of disaster, read in several ways, held together by a promise that his words won't pass away.
what a scholar hears: Daniel's abomination, first Antiochus's altar; cosmic imagery from Isaiah; Mark's own aside to the reader.

sources.quoted: Heaven and earth shall pass away: but my words shall not pass away.

notes: Readings summarized without ranking: preterist (fulfilled in 70), the majority expectation of Christ's return (creeds), futurist (a future tribulation), and the view that 13:14–23 concerns 70 while 24–27 concerns the end. Keeper to confirm fairness.

Antiochus IV's altar (167 BCE) and Hanukkah's rededication (1 Maccabees 4); 'about two centuries before Jesus'. Confirm.
'Mark does something he never does anywhere else': the parenthetical address to the reader in 13:14 is unique in Mark. Confirm.
